contents.html: This report describes NIST’s approach to transitioning from quantum-vulnerable cryptographic algorithms to post-quantum digital signature algorithms and key-establishment schemes. It identifies existing quantum-vulnerable cryptographic standards and the quantum-resistant standards to which information technology products and services will need to transition. It is intended to foster engagement with industry, standards organizations, and relevant agencies to facilitate and accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography. It also supports the implementation of Executive Order 14412 and OMB Memorandum M-26-15, which direct federal agencies to prioritize the migration of their most sensitive systems to post-quantum cryptography.
contents.html_ja: 本報告書は、量子コンピュータに対して脆弱な暗号アルゴリズムから、耐量子デジタル署名アルゴリズムおよび鍵確立方式へ移行するための NIST の取り組み方を説明します。既存の量子脆弱な暗号標準と、情報技術の製品およびサービスが移行すべき量子耐性のある標準を示します。産業界、標準化団体、関係機関との連携を促し、耐量子暗号の採用を円滑にして加速することを意図しています。また、連邦政府機関に最も機微なシステムを優先して耐量子暗号へ移行するよう指示する Executive Order 14412 および OMB Memorandum M-26-15 の実施を支援します。

contents.html: The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in federal information systems.

contents.html: Cryptographic algorithms are vital for safeguarding both the confidentiality and integrity of electronic information. For decades, these algorithms have proved strong enough to defend against attacks using conventional computers that attempt to defeat cryptography. However, future quantum computing may be able to break these algorithms, rendering data and information vulnerable. Countering this future quantum capability requires new cryptographic methods that can protect data from both current conventional computers and the quantum computers of tomorrow. These methods are referred to as post-quantum cryptography (PQC).
contents.html_ja: 暗号アルゴリズムは、電子情報の機密性と完全性の両方を守るうえで不可欠です。これらのアルゴリズムは数十年にわたり、暗号の突破を試みる従来型コンピュータによる攻撃を防ぐのに十分な強度を保ってきました。しかし、将来の量子コンピューティングはこれらのアルゴリズムを破り、データや情報を脆弱にする可能性があります。この将来の量子能力に対抗するには、現在の従来型コンピュータと将来の量子コンピュータの両方からデータを保護できる新しい暗号方式が必要です。これらの方式は耐量子暗号（PQC）と呼ばれます。

contents.html: In response, NIST has released three PQC standards to provide the foundation for the transition to post-quantum cryptography: the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism [FIPS203], the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm [FIPS204], and the Stateless Hash-Based Signature Algorithm [FIPS205]. Historically, the journey from algorithm standardization to full integration into information systems can take 10 to 20 years. This timeline reflects the complexity of companies building the algorithms into products and services, procuring those products and services, and integrating those products and services into technology infrastructures.
contents.html_ja: これを受けて NIST は、耐量子暗号への移行の基盤となる 3 つの PQC 標準を公表しました。モジュール格子ベース鍵カプセル化メカニズム [FIPS203]、モジュール格子ベースデジタル署名アルゴリズム [FIPS204]、ステートレスハッシュベース署名アルゴリズム [FIPS205] です。歴史的に、アルゴリズムの標準化から情報システムへの完全な統合までには 10〜20 年かかることがあります。この期間は、企業がアルゴリズムを製品やサービスに組み込み、それらの製品やサービスを調達し、技術インフラストラクチャに統合する際の複雑さを反映しています。

contents.html: Even though the transition to post-quantum cryptography is starting before a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer has been built, there is a pressing threat. Encrypted data remains at risk because of the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat in which adversaries collect encrypted data now with the goal of decrypting it once quantum technology matures. Since sensitive data often retains its value for many years, starting the transition to post-quantum cryptography now is critical to preventing these future breaches. This threat model is one of the main reasons why the transition to post-quantum cryptography is urgent.
contents.html_ja: 耐量子暗号への移行は、暗号解読に実用上意味のある量子コンピュータが構築される前に始まっていますが、差し迫った脅威があります。「今収集して後で解読する（harvest now, decrypt later）」という脅威のため、暗号化されたデータは依然としてリスクにさらされています。これは、攻撃者が量子技術の成熟後に解読することを目的に、今のうちに暗号化データを収集するというものです。機微なデータは長年にわたって価値を保つことが多いため、将来の侵害を防ぐには、今から耐量子暗号への移行を始めることが重要です。この脅威モデルは、耐量子暗号への移行が急務である主な理由の 1 つです。

contents.html: Executive Order 14412 [EO14412] and OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615] direct federal agencies to execute a risk-prioritized migration that mitigates as much quantum risk as feasible by the end of 2030 and require the Government’s most sensitive systems to adopt PQC for key establishment by December 31, 2030, and for digital signatures by December 31, 2031. Measured against the 10 to 20 years that previous cryptographic transitions have taken, these deadlines leave little margin: meeting them will require immediate and sustained action by federal agencies and by the technology providers, standards organizations, and infrastructure operators on which federal systems depend. Organizations should treat the migration to PQC as a current operational priority, beginning with cryptographic inventories, migration planning, and early deployments of PQC-enabled products and services.
contents.html_ja: Executive Order 14412 [EO14412] と OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615] は、連邦政府機関に対し、2030 年末までに可能な限り多くの量子リスクを軽減するリスク優先の移行を実行するよう指示し、政府の最も機微なシステムに、鍵確立については 2030 年 12 月 31 日までに、デジタル署名については 2031 年 12 月 31 日までに PQC を採用することを求めています。過去の暗号移行に 10〜20 年かかったことと比べると、これらの期限にはほとんど余裕がありません。期限を守るには、連邦政府機関に加え、連邦システムが依存する技術提供者、標準化団体、インフラ運用者による、即時かつ継続的な行動が必要です。組織は、PQC への移行を現在の運用上の優先事項として扱い、暗号の棚卸し、移行計画、PQC 対応の製品およびサービスの早期展開から始めるべきです。

contents.html: Updating cryptographic technology has occurred many times at different scales, such as increasing key sizes or phasing out insecure hash functions and block ciphers. While the transition to PQC is unprecedented in scale, it benefits from a level of awareness and understanding that previous cryptographic changes did not have. NIST recognizes the complexity of migrating the vast array of systems that currently rely on public-key cryptography and acknowledges that this transition will demand substantial effort across diverse applications and infrastructures with specific requirements and constraints.
contents.html_ja: 暗号技術の更新は、鍵長の増加や、安全でないハッシュ関数・ブロック暗号の段階的廃止など、さまざまな規模でこれまで何度も行われてきました。PQC への移行は前例のない規模ですが、過去の暗号変更にはなかったレベルの認識と理解の恩恵を受けています。NIST は、現在公開鍵暗号に依存している膨大な数のシステムを移行することの複雑さを認識しており、この移行が、固有の要件と制約を持つさまざまなアプリケーションやインフラストラクチャにわたって、相当な労力を要することを理解しています。

contents.html: In alignment with the requirements in Executive Order 14412 [EO14412] and OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615], this report serves as the initial step in a broader strategy to manage and guide the transition to post-quantum cryptography. It provides the technical framework necessary to meet the accelerated migration timelines for federal high value assets and high impact systems while serving as a blueprint for critical infrastructure owners and operators and other organizations undergoing the same shift.
contents.html_ja: Executive Order 14412 [EO14412] および OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615] の要件に沿って、本報告書は、耐量子暗号への移行を管理し導くための、より広範な戦略の第一歩となります。連邦政府の重要資産（high value assets）および影響度の高いシステム向けの加速された移行タイムラインを満たすために必要な技術的枠組みを提供するとともに、同様の転換を進める重要インフラの所有者・運用者やその他の組織にとっての青写真としても機能します。

contents.html: This transition will involve the adoption of new PQC algorithms as well as the careful deprecation and eventual removal of quantum-vulnerable algorithms that are currently widespread in technological infrastructures. Public-private engagement will be crucial on the path toward PQC. To facilitate this, the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) Migration to PQC project [NCCOE] provides supporting resources and practical guidelines to assist organizations in managing their cryptographic transition. Additionally, this report continues NIST’s ongoing dialogue with industry, standards organizations, and relevant agencies to develop a clear roadmap and realistic timeline for transitioning to PQC. NIST is committed to ensuring that this transition is as smooth and coordinated as possible, balancing the urgency of adopting PQC with the need to minimize disruption across critical systems. NIST will continue to monitor developments closely and adjust transition efforts as appropriate based on new technological or operational developments. Ultimately, ensuring this smooth transition requires building long-term cryptographic agility into organizational infrastructure to allow for seamless updates as post-quantum standards evolve.
contents.html_ja: この移行では、新しい PQC アルゴリズムを採用するとともに、技術インフラストラクチャに現在広く普及している量子脆弱なアルゴリズムを慎重に非推奨とし、最終的に削除していくことになります。PQC への道筋では、官民の連携が極めて重要です。これを促進するため、国立サイバーセキュリティ卓越センター（NCCoE）の Migration to PQC プロジェクト [NCCOE] は、組織が暗号の移行を管理するのを支援するリソースと実践的なガイドラインを提供しています。さらに本報告書は、PQC への移行に向けた明確なロードマップと現実的なタイムラインを策定するため、産業界、標準化団体、関係機関との NIST の継続的な対話を引き継ぐものです。NIST は、この移行を可能な限り円滑かつ協調的なものにすることに尽力しており、PQC 採用の緊急性と、重要システム全体の混乱を最小限に抑える必要性との均衡を図ります。NIST は引き続き動向を注視し、新たな技術的または運用上の動きに応じて、移行の取り組みを適宜調整します。最終的に、この円滑な移行を確保するには、耐量子標準の進化に応じて途切れなく更新できるよう、長期的な暗号アジリティを組織のインフラストラクチャに組み込む必要があります。

contents.html: NIST-approved digital signature algorithms were historically specified in FIPS 186 [FIPS186]. The current revision of FIPS 186 specifies the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) and adopts the RSA algorithm specified in RFC 8017 (PKCS #1 Version 2.2) and the Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) specified in RFC 8032. The related SP 800-186 [SP800186] specifies the elliptic curves to be used with ECDSA and the elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC)-based key-establishment schemes in SP 800-56A [SP80056A]. These algorithms are vulnerable to Shor’s Algorithm on a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer.

contents.html: SP 800-208, Recommendation for Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes, specifies two stateful hash-based signature (HBS) schemes — the Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) system and the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS) — along with their multi-tree variants, the Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) and multi-tree XMSS (XMSSMT) [SP800208]. These schemes are also resistant to attacks by quantum computers. In stateful hash-based signature (HBS) schemes, the HBS private key consists of a large set of one-time signature (OTS) private keys, either stored directly or deterministically generated as needed from a seed. The security of these schemes relies on the signer to ensure that no individual OTS key is ever used to sign more than one message. Due to this need to maintain state, which requires strict operational controls to track signature indices across distributed systems, stateful HBS schemes are not intended for general use but may be useful for applications like software and firmware signing.

contents.html: SP 800-56A specifies key-establishment schemes based on the discrete logarithm problem over finite fields and elliptic curves, including several variations of Diffie-Hellman and Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (MQV) key-establishment schemes. contents.html: Symmetric-key algorithms (sometimes called secret-key algorithms) use a single key to both apply cryptographic protection and to remove or check the protection (i.e., the same key is used for a cryptographic operation and its inverse). For example, the key used to encrypt data (i.e., apply protection) is also used to decrypt the encrypted data (i.e., remove the protection). In the case of encryption, the original data is called the plaintext, while the encrypted form of the data is called the ciphertext. The key must be kept secret if the data is to remain protected. Several classes of symmetric-key algorithms have been approved: those based on block cipher algorithms (e.g., AES) and those based on the use of hash functions (e.g., a keyed-hash message authentication code based on a hash function).
contents.html_ja: 共通鍵アルゴリズム（シークレット鍵アルゴリズムと呼ばれることもあります）は、暗号による保護の適用と、その保護の除去または検査の両方に単一の鍵を使用します（つまり、暗号操作とその逆操作に同じ鍵が使用されます）。たとえば、データの暗号化（保護の適用）に使用した鍵は、暗号化されたデータの復号（保護の除去）にも使用されます。暗号化の場合、元のデータを平文、データの暗号化された形式を暗号文と呼びます。データを保護されたままにするには、鍵を秘密にしておく必要があります。承認されている共通鍵アルゴリズムには、ブロック暗号アルゴリズム（AES など）に基づくものと、ハッシュ関数の使用に基づくもの（ハッシュ関数に基づく鍵付きハッシュメッセージ認証コードなど）の複数のクラスがあります。

contents.html: Once PQC algorithms have been standardized, applications will need to be modified to make use of them. Many applications include components that are based on standardized protocols and security technologies that will need to be revised to support the use of the PQC algorithms. In addition, applications are built on top of software cryptographic libraries that either provide the implementations of the cryptographic algorithms or provide an interface to hardware cryptographic modules. Any software cryptographic libraries and hardware cryptographic modules used by an application will also need to be revised to support the PQC algorithms. Applications may also rely upon infrastructure components, such as public key infrastructures (PKIs), that would need to be updated to support the PQC algorithms before the applications themselves can migrate to using the PQC algorithms.
contents.html_ja: PQC アルゴリズムが標準化された後は、アプリケーションをそれらを利用するよう修正する必要があります。多くのアプリケーションには、標準化されたプロトコルやセキュリティ技術に基づくコンポーネントが含まれており、PQC アルゴリズムの使用をサポートするために改訂が必要になります。さらに、アプリケーションは、暗号アルゴリズムの実装を提供するか、ハードウェア暗号モジュールへのインターフェースを提供するソフトウェア暗号ライブラリの上に構築されています。アプリケーションが使用するソフトウェア暗号ライブラリやハードウェア暗号モジュールも、PQC アルゴリズムをサポートするよう改訂が必要になります。アプリケーションは、公開鍵基盤（PKI）などのインフラストラクチャコンポーネントにも依存する場合があり、アプリケーション自体が PQC アルゴリズムの使用へ移行できるようになる前に、それらが PQC アルゴリズムをサポートするよう更新される必要があります。

contents.html: These protocols and security technologies often rely on classical cryptographic algorithms that are vulnerable to quantum attacks. Updating them to incorporate PQC algorithms is essential to maintaining data confidentiality and integrity. This involves revising protocol specifications to support new key exchange mechanisms and authentication methods that are quantum-resistant. In some cases, this will involve simply assigning an identifier for the new algorithm. In other cases, more significant changes will be required to accommodate the larger sizes of the PQC algorithms or as a result of the new algorithms having different interfaces.
contents.html_ja: これらのプロトコルとセキュリティ技術は、量子攻撃に対して脆弱な従来の暗号アルゴリズムに依存していることが多くあります。データの機密性と完全性を維持するには、PQC アルゴリズムを組み込むようにそれらを更新することが不可欠です。これには、量子耐性のある新しい鍵交換メカニズムと認証方式をサポートするためのプロトコル仕様の改訂が含まれます。場合によっては、新しいアルゴリズムの識別子を割り当てるだけで済みます。それ以外の場合は、PQC アルゴリズムのサイズが大きいことへの対応や、新しいアルゴリズムのインターフェースが異なることから、より大幅な変更が必要になります。

contents.html: Mosca’s theorem emphasizes the urgency of migrating to post-quantum algorithms by introducing a simple but powerful timeline: if “\(X\)” represents the number of years that data must be kept secure, and “\(Y\)” is the estimated time needed to complete the transition, then organizations must start transitioning to post-quantum algorithms before \(X + Y\) exceeds the expected time \(Z\) for a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer to be built. This means that even if quantum computers are a decade away, organizations must begin the migration to post-quantum cryptography today to avoid having their cryptographically protected data exposed once quantum computers become operational in the future. This threat, often referred to as “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL), underscores the necessity of acting immediately, especially for data with long-term sensitivity, such as government secrets or medical records. Ensuring security today will safeguard it for the future. Consistent with this principle, OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615] directs federal agencies to prioritize the migration of systems that contain data expected to remain mission-sensitive in 2030 alongside high value assets and high impact systems.
contents.html_ja: Mosca の定理は、単純でありながら強力なタイムラインを導入することで、耐量子アルゴリズムへの移行の緊急性を強調しています。データを安全に保つ必要がある年数を「\(X\)」、移行完了に必要な推定時間を「\(Y\)」とすると、\(X + Y\) が、暗号解読に実用上意味のある量子コンピュータが構築されるまでの予想時間 \(Z\) を超える前に、組織は耐量子アルゴリズムへの移行を開始しなければなりません。つまり、量子コンピュータが 10 年先であっても、将来量子コンピュータが稼働したときに暗号で保護されたデータが露出することを避けるため、組織は今日から耐量子暗号への移行を始めなければなりません。「今収集して後で解読する」（HNDL）とよく呼ばれるこの脅威は、特に政府の機密や医療記録のように長期にわたって機微なデータについて、直ちに行動する必要があることを強調しています。今日のセキュリティを確保することが、将来にわたってデータを守ることになります。この原則に沿って、OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615] は、連邦政府機関に対し、重要資産（high value assets）および影響度の高いシステムとともに、2030 年においてもミッション上機微であり続けると見込まれるデータを含むシステムの移行を優先するよう指示しています。

contents.html: Modern network security protocols tend to use separate asymmetric keys for key establishment and authentication. While long-term keys are used for authentication, key-establishment keys are used for a short period of time, usually for a single key-establishment transaction. contents.html: The migration to post-quantum cryptography may initially include hybrid solutions that incorporate the use of quantum-resistant and quantum-vulnerable algorithms when establishing cryptographic keys or generating digital signatures. Hybrid solutions may also refer to solutions that combine multiple PQC key-establishment or digital signature algorithms, which rely on different mathematical assumptions for their security. These hybrid solutions are typically designed to remain secure if at least one of the component algorithms is secure.
contents.html_ja: 耐量子暗号への移行は、当初、暗号鍵の確立やデジタル署名の生成において、量子耐性のあるアルゴリズムと量子脆弱なアルゴリズムの使用を組み合わせたハイブリッドソリューションを含む場合があります。ハイブリッドソリューションは、安全性の根拠とする数学的仮定が異なる複数の PQC 鍵確立アルゴリズムまたはデジタル署名アルゴリズムを組み合わせたソリューションを指す場合もあります。これらのハイブリッドソリューションは通常、構成要素のアルゴリズムの少なくとも 1 つが安全であれば安全性を保つように設計されます。

contents.html: Such hybrid solutions are often utilized as a hedge against a cryptographic or implementation flaw in one of the underlying component algorithms. It may also provide a path for accommodating the use of PQC if sector-specific requirements still require legacy quantum-vulnerable algorithms. However, hybrid solutions add complexity to implementations and architectures, which can increase security risks and costs during the transition to PQC. When used, hybrid solutions are typically expected to be temporary measures that lead to a second transition to cryptographic tools that use only PQC algorithms. Early implementations of new cryptographic algorithms may introduce additional security risks, such as those arising from implementation errors or side-channel vulnerabilities.
contents.html_ja: このようなハイブリッドソリューションは、基盤となる構成要素のアルゴリズムの 1 つにある暗号上または実装上の欠陥に対する備えとして利用されることが多くあります。また、分野固有の要件が依然として従来の量子脆弱なアルゴリズムを求める場合に、PQC の使用に対応する経路となることもあります。しかし、ハイブリッドソリューションは実装とアーキテクチャを複雑にし、PQC への移行中のセキュリティリスクとコストを増大させる可能性があります。使用される場合、ハイブリッドソリューションは通常、PQC アルゴリズムのみを使用する暗号ツールへの第 2 の移行につながる一時的な措置であると想定されます。新しい暗号アルゴリズムの初期の実装は、実装上の誤りやサイドチャネルの脆弱性に起因するものなど、追加のセキュリティリスクをもたらす可能性があります。

contents.html: Whether hybrid solutions are used or not, quantum-vulnerable and quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms will be fielded and used alongside each other in many applications and systems during the transition to PQC to facilitate interoperability. Similarly, during the transition to PQC, PKIs that use quantum-vulnerable digital signature algorithms are expected to be deployed and used alongside those using quantum-resistant algorithms. Such approaches are not considered hybrid solutions if each session only uses a single cryptographic algorithm for key establishment and/or digital signatures.

contents.html: NIST’s cryptography standards provide comprehensive guidance on a broad spectrum of cryptographic mechanisms that are essential for securing sensitive information. These standards cover fundamental areas that are crucial for ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of data, such as encryption algorithms, digital signatures, hash functions, key establishment, and random number generation. Additionally, NIST’s standards define key-management practices and offer frameworks for securely generating, storing, distributing, and destroying cryptographic keys.

NIST has also developed PQC standards to safeguard systems against future quantum attacks. Through collaboration with industry, academia, and other stakeholders, NIST continually updates its cryptographic standards to address evolving security threats and technological advances.

contents.html: National Security Memorandum 10 [NSM10] established 2035 as the target for completing the federal migration to post-quantum cryptography. That overall goal remains in place. Subsequent directives require the Government’s most sensitive systems to migrate substantially earlier. Executive Order 14412 [EO14412] established the policy framework to accelerate the protection of federal systems against quantum threats. This policy is operationalized by OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615], Execution of the Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography, which directs agencies to execute a risk-prioritized migration with the objective of mitigating as much quantum risk as feasible by December 31, 2030. Under this guidance, federal agencies must transition high value assets and high impact systems (i.e., systems for which at least one FIPS 199 security objective is assigned a potential impact value of “high”) on an accelerated schedule. These systems must adopt post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by December 31, 2030, and for digital signatures by December 31, 2031. Agencies must give the same priority to other systems with highly sensitive data or that are likely to be particularly vulnerable to attack by a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer. This includes systems that protect data expected to remain mission-sensitive in 2030. To facilitate the transition to PQC, agencies are also required by Executive Order 14306 [EO14306] and OMB Memorandum M-26-15 to support TLS version 1.3 no later than January 2, 2030.
contents.html_ja: National Security Memorandum 10 [NSM10] は、連邦政府の耐量子暗号への移行を完了する目標として 2035 年を定めました。この全体目標は維持されています。その後の指示により、政府の最も機微なシステムは大幅に早く移行することが求められています。Executive Order 14412 [EO14412] は、量子の脅威に対する連邦システムの保護を加速するための政策枠組みを定めました。この政策は、OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615], Execution of the Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography によって運用化されており、同文書は各機関に対し、2030 年 12 月 31 日までに可能な限り多くの量子リスクを軽減することを目的とした、リスク優先の移行を実行するよう指示しています。このガイダンスのもとで、連邦政府機関は、重要資産（high value assets）と影響度の高いシステム（FIPS 199 のセキュリティ目標の少なくとも 1 つに、潜在的影響度「高」が割り当てられているシステム）を、加速されたスケジュールで移行しなければなりません。これらのシステムは、鍵確立については 2030 年 12 月 31 日までに、デジタル署名については 2031 年 12 月 31 日までに、耐量子暗号を採用しなければなりません。各機関は、非常に機微なデータを扱うシステムや、暗号解読に実用上意味のある量子コンピュータによる攻撃に特に脆弱となる可能性が高いその他のシステムにも、同じ優先度を与えなければなりません。これには、2030 年においてもミッション上機微であり続けると見込まれるデータを保護するシステムが含まれます。PQC への移行を円滑にするため、各機関は Executive Order 14306 [EO14306] と OMB Memorandum M-26-15 により、遅くとも 2030 年 1 月 2 日までに TLS バージョン 1.3 をサポートすることも求められています。

contents.html: The transition schedule in this report is designed to support this risk-based approach. NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. The 2030-2035 deprecation window accommodates lower-risk systems and applications with legacy constraints while full migration concludes. Crucially, this window does not alter the earlier deadlines that apply to high value assets, high impact systems, and other high-sensitivity federal systems under EO 14412 and OMB M-26-15. Systems that cannot support post-quantum cryptography should be identified and prioritized for replacement or decommissioning [OMB2615]. Migration timelines will still vary by use case and application. Systems that protect data with long-term confidentiality needs warrant the earliest transitions, while lower-risk systems may complete migration later in the transition period. NIST will work to ensure that these varying timelines are acknowledged and supported while maintaining the overall goal of completing the migration to post-quantum cryptography by 2035.
contents.html_ja: 本報告書の移行スケジュールは、このリスクベースのアプローチを支援するように設計されています。NIST は、2030 年以降は量子脆弱な公開鍵暗号を非推奨とし、2035 年以降は NIST の標準およびガイドラインにおけるその使用を禁止します。2030〜2035 年の非推奨期間は、完全な移行が完了するまでの間、従来方式の制約を持つリスクの低いシステムやアプリケーションに対応するものです。重要な点として、この期間は、EO 14412 と OMB M-26-15 に基づき重要資産、影響度の高いシステム、その他の機微性の高い連邦システムに適用されるより早い期限を変更するものではありません。耐量子暗号をサポートできないシステムは、特定したうえで、置き換えまたは廃止の優先対象とすべきです [OMB2615]。移行タイムラインは、ユースケースやアプリケーションによって依然として異なります。長期的な機密性が必要なデータを保護するシステムは最も早い移行に値し、リスクの低いシステムは移行期間の後半に移行を完了してもよいです。NIST は、2035 年までに耐量子暗号への移行を完了するという全体目標を維持しつつ、こうした異なるタイムラインが認められ、支援されるよう努めます。

contents.html: Transition schedules are primarily driven by the level of cryptographic protection that a given algorithm and associated parameter set can provide, which is described as a rough measure known as security strength. Historically, the security strength that an algorithm could provide was defined in terms of the amount of work (i.e., the number of operations) that is required to break the algorithm (i.e., an algorithm has \(s\) bits of security strength if breaking the algorithm requires \(2^s\) operations of some kind, where \(s\) = 112, 128, 192, or 256). However, there are significant uncertainties in estimating the security strengths of post-quantum cryptosystems given the difficulty of accurately predicting the performance characteristics of future quantum computers, such as their cost, speed, and memory size.
contents.html_ja: 移行スケジュールは主に、所与のアルゴリズムと関連するパラメータセットが提供できる暗号による保護の水準によって決まります。この水準は、セキュリティ強度と呼ばれる大まかな尺度で表されます。従来、アルゴリズムが提供できるセキュリティ強度は、そのアルゴリズムを破るのに必要な作業量（演算回数）で定義されていました（つまり、アルゴリズムが \(s\) ビットのセキュリティ強度を持つとは、それを破るのに何らかの演算が \(2^s\) 回必要であることをいい、\(s\) = 112、128、192、256 です）。しかし、将来の量子コンピュータのコスト、速度、メモリサイズといった性能特性を正確に予測することが難しいため、耐量子暗号システムのセキュリティ強度の推定には大きな不確実性があります。

contents.html: While NIST guidelines continue to use bit-length security strengths to describe the level of protection offered by an algorithm and parameter set against attacks by classical computers, post-quantum security is described using a collection of broad security categories. Each category is defined by a comparatively easy-to-analyze reference primitive, whose security serves as a floor for a wide variety of metrics that are deemed potentially relevant to practical security. NIST based its classification on the range of security strengths offered by the existing standards in symmetric cryptography. Table 1 provides a summary of these security categories.

contents.html: NIST’s long-term cryptographic algorithm transition plans are outlined in SP 800-57pt1 (Part 1) [SP80057]. These guidelines had projected that NIST would disallow public-key schemes that provide 112 bits of security on January 1, 2031. However, based on the need to migrate to quantum-resistant algorithms during this time frame, NIST will instead deprecate all quantum-vulnerable digital signature algorithms after 2030 and disallow their use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. Organizations may continue using these algorithms and parameter sets as they migrate to the post-quantum signatures identified in Table 3. For federal high value assets, high impact systems, and other systems prioritized under OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615], the continued use of these deprecated algorithms is constrained by the earlier migration deadlines established under EO 14412 [EO14412].

Federal agencies must also comply with OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615], which requires high value assets, high impact systems, and other systems with highly sensitive data to transition to quantum-resistant key establishment by December 31, 2030. contents.html: At this time, ML-KEM is the only approved post-quantum key-establishment scheme based on public-key cryptography. NIST recommends using ML-KEM-768 as the default parameter set, as it provides a large security margin at a reasonable performance cost. In cases where this is impractical or when higher security is required, other parameter sets may be used. As an alternative to ML-KEM, the algorithm HQC was selected for standardization. After publication, HQC will also be an approved post-quantum key-establishment scheme. NIST has no current plans to select any additional KEMs for standardization, although that could change in the future. As noted in Sec. 3.2.1, as long as at least one of the inputs to an approved composite (i.e., hybrid) key-establishment technique comes from an approved key-establishment scheme, the combination can be FIPS 140-validated, even if other inputs are disallowed. Additional guidance on various key combiners is provided in SP 800-227 [SP800227], Recommendations for Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms.

contents.html: NIST’s existing standards in symmetric cryptography — including hash functions [FIPS180][FIPS202][SP800232], XOFs [FIPS202][SP800185][SP800232], block ciphers [FIPS197], KDFs [SP80056C][SP800132][SP800108], AEADs [SP800232], and DRBGs [SP80090A] — are significantly less vulnerable to known quantum attacks than the public-key cryptography standards in SP 800-56A, SP 800-56B, and FIPS 186. In particular, all NIST-approved symmetric primitives that provide at least 128 bits of classical security are believed to meet the requirements of at least Category 1 security within the system of five security strength categories for evaluating parameter sets in the NIST PQC standardization process (see Table 1). NIST has a few symmetric cryptography standards at the 112-bit security level, which will be disallowed in 2030. Applications should move away from these when transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (see SP 800-131A).

contents.html: NIST develops and maintains standards and guidelines that address cryptography used in certain security technologies, protocols, and systems. For example, FIPS 201-3 [FIPS201] and its supporting technical guidelines in NIST Special Publications specify the Personal Identity Verification standard, including security and interoperability requirements for PKI-based credentials used to authenticate federal employees and contractors. Other Special Publications provide guidance on the configuration and use of cryptographic technologies, such as SP 800-52r2 (Revision 2) [SP80052]) on the use of TLS servers and clients. These standards and guidelines are regularly updated to address changes to underlying standards and technologies as well as new threats.
contents.html_ja: NIST は、特定のセキュリティ技術、プロトコル、システムで使用される暗号を扱う標準とガイドラインを策定し、維持しています。たとえば、FIPS 201-3 [FIPS201] と、NIST 特別刊行物にあるそれを支える技術ガイドラインは、連邦職員と請負業者の認証に使用される PKI ベースのクレデンシャルのセキュリティおよび相互運用性の要件を含む、Personal Identity Verification 標準を規定しています。ほかの特別刊行物は、TLS サーバーとクライアントの使用に関する SP 800-52r2（Revision 2）[SP80052] のように、暗号技術の構成と使用に関するガイダンスを提供しています。これらの標準とガイドラインは、基盤となる標準や技術の変化、および新たな脅威に対応するために定期的に更新されています。

contents.html: Throughout the migration to PQC, NIST will revise its documents to provide more detailed guidelines for deprecating quantum-vulnerable algorithms in relevant applications. While NIST’s cryptographic algorithm standards may continue to specify quantum-vulnerable techniques until 2035 and generally allow their use, these application-specific standards and guidelines may specify earlier transitions for certain cryptographic algorithms, techniques, and protocols used within these applications. These guidelines will be developed based on the expected impact that a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer would have on these applications as well as the level of support for PQC in the relevant standards, products, and services. NIST expects to prioritize the migration to quantum-resistant key-establishment schemes within these updates to protect against “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks, particularly in interactive protocols like TLS and Internet Key Exchange (IKE).
contents.html_ja: PQC への移行の全期間を通じて、NIST は、関連するアプリケーションにおける量子脆弱なアルゴリズムの非推奨化について、より詳細なガイドラインを示すため、自らの文書を改訂します。NIST の暗号アルゴリズム標準は 2035 年まで量子脆弱な技術を規定し続け、一般にその使用を許可する場合がありますが、これらのアプリケーション固有の標準およびガイドラインでは、これらのアプリケーション内で使用される特定の暗号アルゴリズム、技術、プロトコルについて、より早い移行を規定する場合があります。これらのガイドラインは、暗号解読に実用上意味のある量子コンピュータがこれらのアプリケーションに与えると予想される影響と、関連する標準、製品、サービスにおける PQC のサポート水準に基づいて策定されます。NIST は、特に TLS や Internet Key Exchange（IKE）のような対話型プロトコルにおいて、「今収集して後で解読する」攻撃から保護するため、これらの更新で量子耐性のある鍵確立方式への移行を優先することを想定しています。

contents.html: TLS is an early priority for the migration as it protects data in transit for nearly every federal system and service, making it a primary target for “harvest now, decrypt later” collection, and agencies are required to support TLS version 1.3 no later than January 2, 2030 [OMB2615]. TLS 1.3 also provides a practical near-term path to quantum-resistant key establishment, including through hybrid key-exchange mechanisms that combine ML-KEM with classical algorithms. Guidance on the use of quantum-resistant key establishment in TLS, including hybrid key-exchange mechanisms, will be reflected in the next revision of SP 800-52 [SP80052].
contents.html_ja: TLS は、ほぼすべての連邦システムとサービスで転送中のデータを保護しているため、移行の初期の優先事項であり、「今収集して後で解読する」攻撃の主な標的になります。また、各機関は遅くとも 2030 年 1 月 2 日までに TLS バージョン 1.3 をサポートすることが求められています [OMB2615]。TLS 1.3 は、ML-KEM と従来のアルゴリズムを組み合わせるハイブリッド鍵交換メカニズムを含め、量子耐性のある鍵確立への実用的な短期的道筋も提供します。ハイブリッド鍵交換メカニズムを含む TLS での量子耐性のある鍵確立の使用に関するガイダンスは、SP 800-52 [SP80052] の次の改訂版に反映されます。

contents.html: Critical trust infrastructure will require significant and sustained effort to migrate in a timely manner. For example, the Personal Identity Verification (PIV) standard [FIPS201] relies on PKI-based credentials whose issuance systems, smart cards, readers, middleware, and supporting public-key infrastructure must all be updated to support PQC algorithms. Because deployed credentials and hardware follow multi-year issuance and replacement cycles, updates to the relevant standards, cryptographic modules, products, and infrastructure must begin early in the transition period for these systems to meet federal migration deadlines. OMB Memorandum M-26-15 similarly directs attention to the modernization of Federal Identity, Credential, and Access Management (FICAM) capabilities in support of PQC [OMB2615].
contents.html_ja: 重要な信頼インフラストラクチャを適時に移行するには、相当で持続的な労力が必要です。たとえば、Personal Identity Verification（PIV）標準 [FIPS201] は PKI ベースのクレデンシャルに依存しており、その発行システム、スマートカード、リーダー、ミドルウェア、支援する公開鍵基盤は、いずれも PQC アルゴリズムをサポートするよう更新しなければなりません。展開済みのクレデンシャルとハードウェアは複数年にわたる発行・交換サイクルに従うため、これらのシステムが連邦政府の移行期限を満たすには、関連する標準、暗号モジュール、製品、インフラストラクチャの更新を移行期間の早い段階で開始しなければなりません。OMB Memorandum M-26-15 も同様に、PQC を支援する Federal Identity, Credential, and Access Management（FICAM）機能の近代化への注力を指示しています [OMB2615]。

Abstract

This report describes NIST’s approach to transitioning from quantum-vulnerable cryptographic algorithms to post-quantum digital signature algorithms and key-establishment schemes. It identifies existing quantum-vulnerable cryptographic standards and the quantum-resistant standards to which information technology products and services will need to transition. It is intended to foster engagement with industry, standards organizations, and relevant agencies to facilitate and accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography. It also supports the implementation of Executive Order 14412 and OMB Memorandum M-26-15, which direct federal agencies to prioritize the migration of their most sensitive systems to post-quantum cryptography.

1. Introduction

Cryptographic algorithms are vital for safeguarding both the confidentiality and integrity of electronic information. For decades, these algorithms have proved strong enough to defend against attacks using conventional computers that attempt to defeat cryptography. However, future quantum computing may be able to break these algorithms, rendering data and information vulnerable. Countering this future quantum capability requires new cryptographic methods that can protect data from both current conventional computers and the quantum computers of tomorrow. These methods are referred to as post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

In response, NIST has released three PQC standards to provide the foundation for the transition to post-quantum cryptography: the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism [FIPS203], the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm [FIPS204], and the Stateless Hash-Based Signature Algorithm [FIPS205]. Historically, the journey from algorithm standardization to full integration into information systems can take 10 to 20 years. This timeline reflects the complexity of companies building the algorithms into products and services, procuring those products and services, and integrating those products and services into technology infrastructures.

Even though the transition to post-quantum cryptography is starting before a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer has been built, there is a pressing threat. Encrypted data remains at risk because of the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat in which adversaries collect encrypted data now with the goal of decrypting it once quantum technology matures. Since sensitive data often retains its value for many years, starting the transition to post-quantum cryptography now is critical to preventing these future breaches. This threat model is one of the main reasons why the transition to post-quantum cryptography is urgent.

Executive Order 14412 [EO14412] and OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615] direct federal agencies to execute a risk-prioritized migration that mitigates as much quantum risk as feasible by the end of 2030 and require the Government’s most sensitive systems to adopt PQC for key establishment by December 31, 2030, and for digital signatures by December 31, 2031. Measured against the 10 to 20 years that previous cryptographic transitions have taken, these deadlines leave little margin: meeting them will require immediate and sustained action by federal agencies and by the technology providers, standards organizations, and infrastructure operators on which federal systems depend. Organizations should treat the migration to PQC as a current operational priority, beginning with cryptographic inventories, migration planning, and early deployments of PQC-enabled products and services.
1.1. Scope and Purpose

Updating cryptographic technology has occurred many times at different scales, such as increasing key sizes or phasing out insecure hash functions and block ciphers. While the transition to PQC is unprecedented in scale, it benefits from a level of awareness and understanding that previous cryptographic changes did not have. NIST recognizes the complexity of migrating the vast array of systems that currently rely on public-key cryptography and acknowledges that this transition will demand substantial effort across diverse applications and infrastructures with specific requirements and constraints.

In alignment with the requirements in Executive Order 14412 [EO14412] and OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615], this report serves as the initial step in a broader strategy to manage and guide the transition to post-quantum cryptography. It provides the technical framework necessary to meet the accelerated migration timelines for federal high value assets and high impact systems while serving as a blueprint for critical infrastructure owners and operators and other organizations undergoing the same shift.

This transition will involve the adoption of new PQC algorithms as well as the careful deprecation and eventual removal of quantum-vulnerable algorithms that are currently widespread in technological infrastructures. Public-private engagement will be crucial on the path toward PQC. To facilitate this, the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) Migration to PQC project [NCCOE] provides supporting resources and practical guidelines to assist organizations in managing their cryptographic transition. Additionally, this report continues NIST’s ongoing dialogue with industry, standards organizations, and relevant agencies to develop a clear roadmap and realistic timeline for transitioning to PQC. NIST is committed to ensuring that this transition is as smooth and coordinated as possible, balancing the urgency of adopting PQC with the need to minimize disruption across critical systems. NIST will continue to monitor developments closely and adjust transition efforts as appropriate based on new technological or operational developments. Ultimately, ensuring this smooth transition requires building long-term cryptographic agility into organizational infrastructure to allow for seamless updates as post-quantum standards evolve.
1.2. Audience

This document is intended for a broad audience, including federal agencies, technology providers, standards organizations, and Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) laboratories. These groups play a critical role in preparing for the migration to PQC by developing, implementing, and standardizing the new cryptographic methods necessary to secure information in the era of quantum computing. This document should inform these efforts and timelines for migrating information technology products, services, and infrastructure to PQC.
2. Background
2.1. Cryptographic Standards

Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) and the NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-series specify a broad set of cryptographic primitives, algorithms, and schemes, including many public-key cryptosystems that will be deprecated and ultimately disallowed as part of the transition to post-quantum cryptography. This section identifies quantum-vulnerable algorithms in NIST’s existing cryptographic standards as well as the post-quantum algorithm standards that have been recently published. Section 4.1 provides the transition plan for the quantum-vulnerable algorithms in these standards.
2.1.1. Digital Signature Algorithms

Digital signature algorithms are used to provide identity authentication, integrity authentication, source authentication, and support for non-repudiation. Digital signature algorithms are used in conjunction with hash functions or eXtendable-Output Functions (XOFs) to sign messages of arbitrary length.

NIST-approved digital signature algorithms were historically specified in FIPS 186 [FIPS186]. The current revision of FIPS 186 specifies the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) and adopts the RSA algorithm specified in RFC 8017 (PKCS #1 Version 2.2) and the Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) specified in RFC 8032. The related SP 800-186 [SP800186] specifies the elliptic curves to be used with ECDSA and the elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC)-based key-establishment schemes in SP 800-56A [SP80056A]. These algorithms are vulnerable to Shor’s Algorithm on a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer.

FIPS 204 and 205 each specify quantum-resistant digital signature schemes. FIPS 204 specifies the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) [FIPS204], which is derived from the CRYSTALS-Dilithium submission. FIPS 205 specifies the Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA), which is derived from the SPHINCS+ submission [FIPS205].

SP 800-208, Recommendation for Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes, specifies two stateful hash-based signature (HBS) schemes — the Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) system and the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS) — along with their multi-tree variants, the Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) and multi-tree XMSS (XMSSMT) [SP800208]. These schemes are also resistant to attacks by quantum computers. In stateful hash-based signature (HBS) schemes, the HBS private key consists of a large set of one-time signature (OTS) private keys, either stored directly or deterministically generated as needed from a seed. The security of these schemes relies on the signer to ensure that no individual OTS key is ever used to sign more than one message. Due to this need to maintain state, which requires strict operational controls to track signature indices across distributed systems, stateful HBS schemes are not intended for general use but may be useful for applications like software and firmware signing.

NIST is developing a FIPS that specifies a digital signature algorithm derived from FALCON as an additional alternative to these standards. NIST is also evaluating other proposed digital signature algorithms for possible standardization through the Additional Digital Signature Schemes for the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization Process [NISTIR8528].
2.1.2. Key Establishment

Key establishment is the means by which keys are generated and provided to the entities that are authorized to use them. Current NIST-approved key-establishment schemes are specified in SP 800-56A, Recommendation for Pair-Wise Key-Establishment Schemes Using Discrete Logarithm-Based Cryptography [SP80056A], and SP 800-56B, Recommendation for Pair-Wise Key-Establishment Schemes Using Integer Factorization Cryptography [SP80056B].

SP 800-56A specifies key-establishment schemes based on the discrete logarithm problem over finite fields and elliptic curves, including several variations of Diffie-Hellman and Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (MQV) key-establishment schemes. SP 800-56B specifies key-establishment schemes based on the RSA public key cryptosystem. This publication includes approved methods for both key agreement and key transport. The key-establishment algorithms in both of these Special Publications are vulnerable to Shor’s Algorithm on a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer.

FIPS 203 specifies a cryptographic scheme called Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), which is derived from the CRYSTALS-KYBER submission. A key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) is a particular type of key-establishment scheme that can be used to establish a shared secret key between two parties communicating over a public channel. The fourth round of the NIST PQC Standardization process evaluated additional KEM algorithms, and NIST selected HQC as an alternative to ML-KEM [NISTIR8545]. A FIPS that specifies HQC-KEM is under development.
2.1.3. Symmetric Cryptography

Symmetric-key algorithms (sometimes called secret-key algorithms) use a single key to both apply cryptographic protection and to remove or check the protection (i.e., the same key is used for a cryptographic operation and its inverse). For example, the key used to encrypt data (i.e., apply protection) is also used to decrypt the encrypted data (i.e., remove the protection). In the case of encryption, the original data is called the plaintext, while the encrypted form of the data is called the ciphertext. The key must be kept secret if the data is to remain protected. Several classes of symmetric-key algorithms have been approved: those based on block cipher algorithms (e.g., AES) and those based on the use of hash functions (e.g., a keyed-hash message authentication code based on a hash function).
Symmetric-key algorithms are used for:
Encryption using block cipher modes of operation
Data authentication using block cipher modes of operation
Data authentication using keyed-hash constructions
Key derivation
Key wrapping
Random bit generation

As discussed in Sec. 4.1.3, the existing algorithm standards for symmetric cryptography are less vulnerable to attacks by quantum computers. NIST does not expect to need to transition away from these standards as part of the PQC migration.
2.2. Cryptographic Technologies and Components

Once PQC algorithms have been standardized, applications will need to be modified to make use of them. Many applications include components that are based on standardized protocols and security technologies that will need to be revised to support the use of the PQC algorithms. In addition, applications are built on top of software cryptographic libraries that either provide the implementations of the cryptographic algorithms or provide an interface to hardware cryptographic modules. Any software cryptographic libraries and hardware cryptographic modules used by an application will also need to be revised to support the PQC algorithms. Applications may also rely upon infrastructure components, such as public key infrastructures (PKIs), that would need to be updated to support the PQC algorithms before the applications themselves can migrate to using the PQC algorithms.
2.2.1. Network Protocol and Security Technology Standards

Network protocols and security technology standards define the rules for data exchange over networks and ensure secure and reliable communication. Examples include Transport Layer Security (TLS), Secure Shell (SSH), Internet Protocol Security (IPsec), and Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).

These protocols and security technologies often rely on classical cryptographic algorithms that are vulnerable to quantum attacks. Updating them to incorporate PQC algorithms is essential to maintaining data confidentiality and integrity. This involves revising protocol specifications to support new key exchange mechanisms and authentication methods that are quantum-resistant. In some cases, this will involve simply assigning an identifier for the new algorithm. In other cases, more significant changes will be required to accommodate the larger sizes of the PQC algorithms or as a result of the new algorithms having different interfaces.
2.2.2. Software Cryptographic Libraries

Software cryptographic libraries are collections of cryptographic algorithms and protocols that are implemented in software to provide essential cryptographic functions to applications. OpenSSL, BoringSSL, and Libsodium are a few examples of cryptographic libraries that are used to provide cryptographic support for applications.

These libraries need to incorporate PQC algorithms that are standardized by bodies like NIST. Updating the libraries ensures that developers have access to quantum-resistant cryptographic functions without implementing complex algorithms themselves. This transition involves adding new algorithms, optimizing their implementations for performance, and ensuring that those implementations are secure against side-channel attacks.
2.2.3. Cryptographic Hardware

Cryptographic hardware modules, such as hardware security modules (HSMs) and Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs), provide secure environments for performing cryptographic operations and storing sensitive keys. They are used in various applications, from securing server infrastructure to protecting cryptographic keys on personal devices.

Hardware modules must be upgraded or redesigned to support PQC algorithms, which often have larger key sizes and different computational requirements. This includes updating firmware or hardware to handle new algorithms and ensuring that the modules can perform quantum-resistant cryptographic operations efficiently while maintaining the high security standards expected of these devices and ensuring that PQC algorithms are always used to provide security-critical services, such as protecting the integrity of software and firmware updates. Given the extensive lead times for hardware research, design, and fabrication, it is a high priority for vendors to initiate the integration of PQC support immediately. This ensures that hardware availability will coincide with the broader ecosystem migration.
2.2.4. PKI and Other Infrastructure Components

Public key infrastructure (PKI) systems manage digital certificates and public-private key pairs to enable secure communication and authentication across networks. Other infrastructure components include certification authorities (CAs), registration authorities, key management systems, and directory services.

PKI components must be updated to issue, distribute, and manage certificates that use PQC algorithms and to sign certificates and revocation status information using PQC algorithms. This includes supporting new cryptographic algorithms (possibly including hybrid signature schemes; see Sec. 3.2.2) in certificate issuance processes and modifying validation and revocation mechanisms. Ensuring backward compatibility and interoperability during the transition period is crucial to maintaining trust and security across a network.
2.2.5. IT Applications and Services

IT applications and services encompass a wide array of software and platforms used by organizations, including web applications, databases, communication tools, cloud services, and enterprise software. These applications rely on cryptography for securing data, authenticating users, and ensuring secure transactions.

Applications and services must be modified to support PQC algorithms for encryption, digital signatures, and key establishment. This requires updating the underlying cryptographic implementations, adjusting to changes in key sizes and algorithm performance, and ensuring compatibility with updated protocols and libraries. Developers need to refactor code, conduct extensive testing, and potentially redesign user interfaces to accommodate these changes.
3. Migration Considerations

Even though there are no existing cryptanalytically relevant quantum computers that currently threaten levels of security, it will take a significant amount of time to transition to new post-quantum algorithms. Past cryptographic migrations have taken over a decade, and this more complex migration will likely take at least that long. There will be an extended period during which both older quantum-vulnerable algorithms and their PQC replacements will coexist and be validated by NIST. As directed by Executive Order 14412 [EO14412], NIST is also revising Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) processes to accelerate the validation of cryptographic modules that implement PQC algorithms.

Mosca’s theorem emphasizes the urgency of migrating to post-quantum algorithms by introducing a simple but powerful timeline: if “X” represents the number of years that data must be kept secure, and “Y” is the estimated time needed to complete the transition, then organizations must start transitioning to post-quantum algorithms before X + Y exceeds the expected time Z for a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer to be built. This means that even if quantum computers are a decade away, organizations must begin the migration to post-quantum cryptography today to avoid having their cryptographically protected data exposed once quantum computers become operational in the future. This threat, often referred to as “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL), underscores the necessity of acting immediately, especially for data with long-term sensitivity, such as government secrets or medical records. Ensuring security today will safeguard it for the future. Consistent with this principle, OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615] directs federal agencies to prioritize the migration of systems that contain data expected to remain mission-sensitive in 2030 alongside high value assets and high impact systems.

While signatures are not vulnerable to HNDL attacks, transitioning to post-quantum signatures is also urgent due to the longer duration and greater complexity of the transition process and the need for a greater number of parties to coordinate.
3.1. Use Cases
3.1.1. Code Signing

Code signing involves digitally signing executables and software packages to verify the author’s identity and ensure that the code has not been tampered with. This process is critical for maintaining trust in software distribution channels and preventing the spread of malicious code.

The devices that install and execute this code need the ability to verify the signatures on the code. In some cases, it is not feasible to update the code that performs the signature verification after the devices have been manufactured. When this is the case, it is important for the devices to be designed to require quantum-resistant signatures on the executable code if there is a risk that the devices will still be in use after cryptanalytically relevant quantum computers become available.
3.1.2. User and Machine Authentication

User and machine authentication systems verify identities to control access to resources. This often involves cryptographic protocols that use asymmetric algorithms for secure key exchange and authentication, ensuring that only authorized users or devices can access sensitive data or services. Depending on the protocol, authentication may be performed using either a digital signature algorithm or a key-establishment scheme.

Unlike with encryption, where there is a threat of HNDL, an authentication system remains secure as long as the cryptographic algorithms and keys used to perform the authentication are secure when the authentication is performed. Authentication systems may continue to use quantum-vulnerable algorithms until quantum computers that are capable of breaking current, quantum-vulnerable algorithms become available, at which point authentication using these algorithms will need to immediately transition to the use of quantum-resistant algorithms.

Supporting quantum-resistant algorithms for authentication will require upgrades to both the system performing and accepting the authentication, as well as to any supporting infrastructure, such as a PKI. Transitioning may also require obtaining hardware cryptographic tokens that support the quantum-resistant algorithms.
3.1.3. Network Security Protocols

Network security protocols like TLS and virtual private networks secure data transmission over public networks. They use cryptographic techniques to provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication between communicating parties.

Modern network security protocols tend to use separate asymmetric keys for key establishment and authentication. While long-term keys are used for authentication, key-establishment keys are used for a short period of time, usually for a single key-establishment transaction. This provides the property of forward secrecy, where the compromise of a long-term key does not result in the compromise of communication sessions that occurred before the compromise.

As symmetric keys that are established through the key-establishment process are used to provide confidentiality, the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat needs to be considered when determining a migration timeline for the key-establishment scheme.
The cryptographic algorithm used for authentication may be transitioned at a different time, and for that, the considerations in Sec. 3.1.2 apply.
3.1.4. Email and Document Signing and Encryption

Email, PDF files, and document signing employ digital signatures to verify the authenticity and integrity of electronic communications and documents. Common algorithms like RSA and ECDSA are widely used to create a cryptographic binding between the content and the sender’s identity, ensuring that the message has not been altered and that it originates from a legitimate source.

Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) and OpenPGP are standards for public-key encryption and the signing of MIME data. It provides end-to-end encryption and authentication for email and file exchanges to ensure that only intended recipients can access the content. As with other applications providing data confidentiality, email encryption is subject to HNDL.
3.2. PQC-Classical Hybrid Protocols

The migration to post-quantum cryptography may initially include hybrid solutions that incorporate the use of quantum-resistant and quantum-vulnerable algorithms when establishing cryptographic keys or generating digital signatures. Hybrid solutions may also refer to solutions that combine multiple PQC key-establishment or digital signature algorithms, which rely on different mathematical assumptions for their security. These hybrid solutions are typically designed to remain secure if at least one of the component algorithms is secure.

Such hybrid solutions are often utilized as a hedge against a cryptographic or implementation flaw in one of the underlying component algorithms. It may also provide a path for accommodating the use of PQC if sector-specific requirements still require legacy quantum-vulnerable algorithms. However, hybrid solutions add complexity to implementations and architectures, which can increase security risks and costs during the transition to PQC. When used, hybrid solutions are typically expected to be temporary measures that lead to a second transition to cryptographic tools that use only PQC algorithms. Early implementations of new cryptographic algorithms may introduce additional security risks, such as those arising from implementation errors or side-channel vulnerabilities.

These trade-offs will vary based on the hybrid techniques used, the applications involved, and the vendor and user communities that will develop and deploy them. Implementers and standards organizations that specify cryptographic protocols and technologies need to carefully consider the security, costs, and complexity of hybrid solutions in their environments.

Industry and standards organizations are considering a variety of techniques for hybrid solutions with key-establishment schemes and digital signatures. NIST intends to accommodate the use of hybrid techniques in its cryptographic standards to facilitate the transition to PQC where their use is desired.

Whether hybrid solutions are used or not, quantum-vulnerable and quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms will be fielded and used alongside each other in many applications and systems during the transition to PQC to facilitate interoperability. For example, many network security protocols support the use of multiple sets of cryptographic algorithms and allow two communicating parties to negotiate which algorithms to use in each session. Similarly, during the transition to PQC, PKIs that use quantum-vulnerable digital signature algorithms are expected to be deployed and used alongside those using quantum-resistant algorithms. Such approaches are not considered hybrid solutions if each session only uses a single cryptographic algorithm for key establishment and/or digital signatures.

NIST leaves the decision to each specific application as to whether it can afford the implementation cost, performance reduction, and engineering complexity (including proper and independent security reviews) of a hybrid mode for key establishment or the use of dual signatures. To assist external parties that desire such a mechanism, NIST will accommodate the use of a hybrid key-establishment mode and dual signatures in FIPS 140 validation when suitably combined with a NIST-approved scheme.
3.2.1. Hybrid Key-Establishment Techniques

A hybrid key-establishment mode is defined here to be a key-establishment scheme that is a combination of two or more components that are themselves cryptographic key-establishment schemes. The hybrid key-establishment scheme becomes a composite of these component schemes.

NIST currently allows a generic composite key-establishment technique described in SP 800-56C [SP80056C]. Assume that the value Z is a shared secret that was generated as specified by SP 800-56A or SP 800-56B and that a shared secret T is generated or distributed through other schemes. The value Z’=Z||T may then be treated as a shared secret and any of the key derivation methods given in SP 800-56C may be applied to Z’ to derive secret keying material.

NIST intends to update SP 800-56C so that the value Z may be generated as specified by any current and future NIST key-establishment standards. This will include SP 800-56A, SP 800-56B, FIPS 203, and any additional post-quantum key-establishment standards. The generic composite key-establishment technique is allowed, even if T is derived from an unapproved source (including a disallowed algorithm). SP 800-56C will also be updated to reflect that the ordering of Z and T can be reversed (i.e., Z’=T||Z is also allowed1).

The desired property of hybrid techniques is that derived keys remain secure if at least one of the component schemes is secure. Security properties can be complex, and for composite key-establishment schemes, they will need to be analyzed on a case-by-case basis with the requirements of the application in mind. NIST offers guidance on various key combiners in SP 800-227 [SP800227], Recommendations for Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms.

Additionally, the output of the key-establishment scheme specified in FIPS 203 is a shared secret key, which is a shared secret that does not require further key derivation. NIST emphasizes that any shared secret key generated as specified in FIPS 203 may be used as the value Z in the generic composite mode described in SP 800-56C. These same properties will apply to any future FIPS that standardize KEMs.
3.2.2. Hybrid Digital Signature Techniques

Common techniques for hybrid digital signatures involve the use of dual signatures, which consist of two or more signatures on a common message. It may also be known as a hybrid signature or composite signature. The verification of the dual signature requires all of the component signatures to be successfully verified, such as by creating a single logical composite signature from two or more component signature algorithms. As in the case of hybrid key-establishment, the security properties of hybrid signatures are complex and need to be carefully analyzed.
1 The order of the shared secrets will need to be specified at the protocol level to avoid confusion.

Dual signatures could be used to sign user data (e.g., a document, e-mail) or digital certificates that contain references to user key pairs within a PKI. Existing NIST standards and guidelines accommodate their use provided that at least one component digital signature algorithm is NIST-approved.
4. PQC Standards Transition Timeline

NIST’s cryptography standards provide comprehensive guidance on a broad spectrum of cryptographic mechanisms that are essential for securing sensitive information. These standards cover fundamental areas that are crucial for ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of data, such as encryption algorithms, digital signatures, hash functions, key establishment, and random number generation. Additionally, NIST’s standards define key-management practices and offer frameworks for securely generating, storing, distributing, and destroying cryptographic keys.

Beyond individual algorithms, NIST standards provide guidance on cryptographic protocols that secure communications, such as the TLS protocol, which protects internet data exchanges. They also specify requirements for cryptographic modules validated by the CMVP to ensure that implementations meet stringent security standards. NIST has also developed PQC standards to safeguard systems against future quantum attacks. Through collaboration with industry, academia, and other stakeholders, NIST continually updates its cryptographic standards to address evolving security threats and technological advances.

National Security Memorandum 10 [NSM10] established 2035 as the target for completing the federal migration to post-quantum cryptography. That overall goal remains in place. Subsequent directives require the Government’s most sensitive systems to migrate substantially earlier. Executive Order 14412 [EO14412] established the policy framework to accelerate the protection of federal systems against quantum threats. This policy is operationalized by OMB Memorandum M-26-15 [OMB2615], Execution of the Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography, which directs agencies to execute a risk-prioritized migration with the objective of mitigating as much quantum risk as feasible by December 31, 2030. Under this guidance, federal agencies must transition high value assets and high impact systems (i.e., systems for which at least one FIPS 199 security objective is assigned a potential impact value of “high”) on an accelerated schedule. These systems must adopt post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by December 31, 2030, and for digital signatures by December 31, 2031. Agencies must give the same priority to other systems with highly sensitive data or that are likely to be particularly vulnerable to attack by a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer. This includes systems that protect data expected to remain mission-sensitive in 2030. To facilitate the transition to PQC, agencies are also required by Executive Order 14306 [EO14306] and OMB Memorandum M-26-15 to support TLS version 1.3 no later than January 2, 2030.

The transition schedule in this report is designed to support this risk-based approach. NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. The 2030-2035 deprecation window accommodates lower-risk systems and applications with legacy constraints while full migration concludes. Crucially, this window does not alter the earlier deadlines that apply to high value assets, high impact systems, and other high-sensitivity federal systems under EO 14412 and OMB M-26-15. Systems that cannot support post-quantum cryptography should be identified and prioritized for replacement or decommissioning [OMB2615]. Migration timelines will still vary by use case and application. Systems that protect data with long-term confidentiality needs warrant the earliest transitions, while lower-risk systems may complete migration later in the transition period. NIST will work to ensure that these varying timelines are acknowledged and supported while maintaining the overall goal of completing the migration to post-quantum cryptography by 2035.
4.1. NIST Cryptographic Algorithm Standards and Guidelines

SP 800-131A [SP800131A][SP800131A] describes the transitions associated with the use of cryptography by Federal Government agencies to protect controlled unclassified information. The document addresses the use of algorithms and key lengths specified in FIPS and NIST SPs. During the transition to post-quantum cryptography, NIST will revise SP 800-131A with more detailed guidelines and schedules.
The terms “acceptable,” “deprecated, “disallowed,” and “legacy use” are used throughout SP 800-131A to indicate the approval status of an algorithm:
Acceptable means that the algorithm and key length/ strength in a FIPS or SP are approved for use in accordance with any associated guidance.

Deprecated means that the algorithm and key length/strength may be used, but there is some security risk. The data owner must examine this risk potential and decide whether to continue to use a deprecated algorithm or key length.
Disallowed means that the algorithm, key length/strength, parameter set, or scheme is no longer allowed for the stated purpose.
Legacy use means that the algorithm, scheme, or parameter set may only be used to process already protected information (e.g., to decrypt ciphertext data or to verify a digital signature).

Transition schedules are primarily driven by the level of cryptographic protection that a given algorithm and associated parameter set can provide, which is described as a rough measure known as security strength. Historically, the security strength that an algorithm could provide was defined in terms of the amount of work (i.e., the number of operations) that is required to break the algorithm (i.e., an algorithm has s bits of security strength if breaking the algorithm requires 2s operations of some kind, where s = 112, 128, 192, or 256). However, there are significant uncertainties in estimating the security strengths of post-quantum cryptosystems given the difficulty of accurately predicting the performance characteristics of future quantum computers, such as their cost, speed, and memory size.

While NIST guidelines continue to use bit-length security strengths to describe the level of protection offered by an algorithm and parameter set against attacks by classical computers, post-quantum security is described using a collection of broad security categories. Each category is defined by a comparatively easy-to-analyze reference primitive, whose security serves as a floor for a wide variety of metrics that are deemed potentially relevant to practical security. NIST based its classification on the range of security strengths offered by the existing standards in symmetric cryptography. Table 1 provides a summary of these security categories.

original_blocks.html: 4.2. Application-Specific Standards and Guidelines

NIST develops and maintains standards and guidelines that address cryptography used in certain security technologies, protocols, and systems. For example, FIPS 201-3 [FIPS201] and its supporting technical guidelines in NIST Special Publications specify the Personal Identity Verification standard, including security and interoperability requirements for PKI-based credentials used to authenticate federal employees and contractors. Other Special Publications provide guidance on the configuration and use of cryptographic technologies, such as SP 800-52r2 (Revision 2) [SP80052]) on the use of TLS servers and clients. These standards and guidelines are regularly updated to address changes to underlying standards and technologies as well as new threats.

Throughout the migration to PQC, NIST will revise its documents to provide more detailed guidelines for deprecating quantum-vulnerable algorithms in relevant applications. While NIST’s cryptographic algorithm standards may continue to specify quantum-vulnerable techniques until 2035 and generally allow their use, these application-specific standards and guidelines may specify earlier transitions for certain cryptographic algorithms, techniques, and protocols used within these applications. These guidelines will be developed based on the expected impact that a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer would have on these applications as well as the level of support for PQC in the relevant standards, products, and services. NIST expects to prioritize the migration to quantum-resistant key-establishment schemes within these updates to protect against “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks, particularly in interactive protocols like TLS and Internet Key Exchange (IKE).

TLS is an early priority for the migration as it protects data in transit for nearly every federal system and service, making it a primary target for “harvest now, decrypt later” collection, and agencies are required to support TLS version 1.3 no later than January 2, 2030 [OMB2615]. TLS 1.3 also provides a practical near-term path to quantum-resistant key establishment, including through hybrid key-exchange mechanisms that combine ML-KEM with classical algorithms. Guidance on the use of quantum-resistant key establishment in TLS, including hybrid key-exchange mechanisms, will be reflected in the next revision of SP 800-52 [SP80052].

Critical trust infrastructure will require significant and sustained effort to migrate in a timely manner. For example, the Personal Identity Verification (PIV) standard [FIPS201] relies on PKI-based credentials whose issuance systems, smart cards, readers, middleware, and supporting public-key infrastructure must all be updated to support PQC algorithms. Because deployed credentials and hardware follow multi-year issuance and replacement cycles, updates to the relevant standards, cryptographic modules, products, and infrastructure must begin early in the transition period for these systems to meet federal migration deadlines. OMB Memorandum M-26-15 similarly directs attention to the modernization of Federal Identity, Credential, and Access Management (FICAM) capabilities in support of PQC [OMB2615].

NIST will also coordinate with standards-developing organizations and industry to ensure that critical security protocols and technologies are updated to support PQC in a timely manner, recognizing that different application areas will have different risks, security needs, and adoption challenges.
